cards.title: Blender's UI and Runtime: Much Faster Than GPUI

depth.text: someone turned **Blender's interface** into a **reusable UI library** for apps written in different languages

BUI pulls **Blender's widget drawing and interaction rules** into a **standalone library** with a small C core. The README says its benchmark uses **2–4× less CPU per frame** than gpui-fast, with less RAM and a ~5 ms first frame.

cards.camps: Two camps: some want Blender's UI in more apps; others don't want it outside Blender and say its GPL license restricts use.

comments.text: Can I please congratulate you on your README. It rapidly tells me what I'm looking at, and why I might be interested in the project. There are so many READMEs around that ... just don't do that. They ramble about technical implementation details, how their language choice is amazing, and a third of the way through the README, I'm still left wondering, "but what does this project do?".

I love the general idea behind Blender's UI. And I do appreciate the effort that goes into it, especially in the latest versions as it got much better, But I really really really REALLY don't want that UI in anything else other than Blender. Please don't.

That's really cool! I burned some tokens trying to develop something similar but gave up halfway. A lot of people criticize Blender's UI but as someone who has been using blender for more than a decade now I just find it so elegant. Just the customizability itself is something I miss on most 3D software, if not all of them. Being able to just split screens and change their functionality, paired…

For anyone looking at Rust GUI: don't expect GPUI to be the fastest. From what I've heard, Iced, Slint, Dioxus Native, Freya, etc are all faster. Despite claims of being blazingly fast, GPUI isn't that optimized. Zed gets away with it because it's UI is simple.
It would be such a boon if GIMP and Inkscape could adopt blender's fantastic GUI

ASN says **iDEAL | Wero** isn't supported on every device or operating system, offers **no workaround**, and is still investigating support for alternatives. EPI says **Google Play Integrity** checks app and operating-system integrity for payment security.

cards.title: Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production

depth.text: Tesla is winding down the **Cybertruck** after **weak sales**, making room for more Cybercabs

Tesla says production at its Texas gigafactory will wind down around **mid-2027**, so it can make more of its newly launched **Cybercab**. It sold **20,237 Cybertrucks** in the US last year, down 48% from 38,965 in 2024; Musk had predicted annual sales of 250,000 before launch.

cards.camps: Two camps: critics say it was overpriced or impractical; fans say its unusual design made it fun and fresh.

He'd run the house on it for a couple of days, then drive the cybertruck over to a super charger station, recharge, then come home and plug the house back in. The battery capacity on those things is equivalent to 9 Tesla…

There are a lot of lenses through which to view the failure of the cybertruck: aesthetics, not enough truck not enough SUV, size, association of aesthetics with politics, etc. But I think the main one that is ignored is price. The cybertruck was built in an era of high truck prices driven by zero interest rates. It bet on the price of trucks going up, just as the Ford F150 electric did. That was…

- Federal EV tax credits are over. - The emissions credit market (where Tesla made most of its money) is dead due to lowered standards. - Manufacturing costs haven't come down. - EV sales share in the US is down to 6% (and falling every quarter). - Chinese EVs are dominating every market outside the US. - All the overhyped moonshots (sub-$30K car, unsupervised autopilot, autonomous robots) are…

From my perspective, owning a truck and SUV and using them differently for various use cases, the cybertruck is neither. So even if I ignore everything else I feel about it’s aesthetic, Musk, politics, etc. It simply does not serve many real world needs that I have. It put itself in a very narrow box of, only people that really like this quirky design and also like/feel indifferent to the…

The absurdity is the best part of it. Finally it was something new, in a landscape where every car and truck has looked the same for the past 20 years. I'm happy someone designed and built something so crazy and different. It probably would have been better had they not been mass produced, and maybe did a very limited quantity run - make it more like a collector item... I suppose thats what it'll…

depth.text: Britain plans to require **salary details** in job ads, and commenters debate whether **ranges help**

A commenter quotes **Burnham's office** saying legislation will go to parliament soon, but gives no timeline. Supporters say salary ranges could save applicants time; others worry **very wide ranges** could make the disclosure useless.

cards.camps: Two camps: supporters say disclosure saves time and may reduce pay inequality; skeptics worry broad ranges could be useless or narrow rules too rigid.

cards.title: From Linux to Wikipedia: How Volunteers Build the Internet

depth.text: the post explores how **volunteers** helped build the **Internet**, from Linux to Wikipedia

The comments call this **peer production**: projects can draw on volunteers, paid engineers, and organizations that contribute or donate. Some readers say mixing voluntary work with financial gains makes the story less simple.

cards.camps: Two camps: some emphasize volunteers and community effort; others point to paid corporate work, with one commenter crediting the U.S. DoD for building the Internet.

comments.text: Things were build by passionate people, who had the skills and the means to do it. I feel that modern tech first took away the passion, by making everything a product, than took away the means by making everything cloud, and now kills the skills by eutrophizing our brains with AI. There is no cabal of evil tech that pushes this, but the results are the same.

While a lot of this involved volunteers and people taking initiative, a lot of this is also people working and being paid to do so. Linus Torvalds was getting paid to work on the Linux kernel from pretty early on, for example. And a lot of contributions made to Linux are done by software engineers working for a very wide range of companies that each have their own commercial interest in moving…

I love these two projects for how they are, and continue to be, built. They say something hopeful and deep about humanity. Before Linux and Wikipedia, we assumed that if you gave everyone a sharpie, that we would graffiti and deface the world. Instead, we learned that humans will stop and sit and write the most thorough history ever seen for the sake of free knowledge and create the tools for us…

This has happened with most of the fields - volunteers do a lot of work, make their fields/areas good, raise interest, bring ppl into it which usually brings money then which usually brings money chasers who then usually "optimize" the hell out of every metric for maximum gains. Great OS volunteers still exist today, but the ratio of genuine field lover to money chaser is absurd now.
Excellent reminder. It very often feels like this place forgets where most of the good stuff comes from.

cards.title: Kugelblitz – Mac-Native Google Earth Alternative

depth.text: someone built a **Mac globe app** for flying over terrain, maps, and **open geodata**

Kugelblitz layers imagery, road and topographic maps over **real terrain**, with **3D buildings**; its atlas view flattens the same data in five projections. It also computes eclipses over **5,000 years**, alongside earthquakes, eruptions, tsunamis and fireballs at their place and time.

cards.camps: Some report it works fine on an M1 Pro; others mock the claim that it flies smoothly even on an M1, noting Google Earth was smooth on much older computers.

cards.title: $2.5T has been wiped from US stocks

depth.text: US stocks shed **$2.5T on paper**, while commenters debate **what caused the drop**

One commenter says **the headline's $2.5T is market-cap math**: it multiplies the marginal share price by all shares, which isn't the same as adding up what those shares would sell for individually. Another says the election link may be **a convenient coincidence**.

cards.camps: Some commenters connect the drop to election-related expectations; others say the timing may be coincidence and a day's move is hard to pin on one cause.

comments.text:
For all the federal election related takes, remember that 1. Market price changes are changes from what was expected before compared to what is expected now. And not even only in regards to the asset itself, but with respect to comparative change in other assets as well.
2. conventional wisdom when the branches of government are divided, less change comes from the government, so you can expect…

I always find these market cap numbers misleading. The US stock market isn't "worth" $2.5T less. If you multiply the marginal share price by the total number of shares, you get a number that's $2.5T lower. That is something different. E.g., if you tried to sell all Nvidia shares at once, you'd never get anywhere near ~$4.5T (just as buying them all would cost far more).

This is definitely scary, but not the end of the world (yet). The S&P500 is still up ~7% YTD, and 5y CAGR of 9.4% before dividends, in line with historical norms. This is primarily a decline in tech: week over week, the S&P is -4.5% (SPX), but the S&P excluding tech is +0.1% (SPXT). Right now, this looks like speculation that tech will reduce capex after Q4 earnings (Nvidia, Micron, Sandisk, AMD…

cards.title: Claude Code sends your email address to websites

cards.title: Obscure audio codec is a perfect fit for the N64

depth.text: someone got an **obscure audio codec** playing N64 music without **hogging the CPU**
The author ported ULC’s decoder to the **N64’s RSP**, with **Codex** helping translate C into RSPL. It handles 44100 Hz stereo using about **4% of CPU time** and 5% of RSP time.

cards.camps: Two camps: the article says MP3 decoding hurt Conker's frame rate; one commenter says raw RDP fillrate issues were mainly to blame.

comments.text: This codec would have been great 27 years ago! I suspect it wouldn't have gotten past the patent lawyers in 1999 though. It seems cute today but the entire codec space was a patent minefield, the N64 mp3 decoder was implemented twice (once based on the reference codec, once clean) with Nintendo/Rare then paying RAD game tools to license their decoder... of which none of their code was used but…

In case anyone else got to the demo thinking the quality is awful -- the vocals are incomprehensible and keep cutting out -- it turns out it's like that in the original track: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i1gVxKhdGPs&t=57s

I wonder if this would also be a great fit for the MAS3507D! Supposedly you can replace the program with your own in a 1-kiloword RAM (the default MP3 decoder is in ROM, and probably larger). If you can fit this codec in 1024 MIPS instructions, perhaps you can do the same in 1024 of these DSP instructions… Too bad there is seemingly zero public documentation on the format of these programs…
It was all great until they mentioned LLM usage. The demoscene and homebrew scene is dying as we speak.

cards.title: Inkling 2 Small

glossary.GPU: Graphics Processing Unit: the chip part that draws images and video.

glossary.Accessibility access: A Mac permission that lets an app see which window is currently focused.
glossary.private macOS window APIs: Application Programming Interfaces: ways an app asks macOS to do things; private ones are not meant for every app to use.
glossary.notarized: Checked by Apple for known security problems before an app is distributed.
glossary.Hackintosh: A way to run macOS on computer hardware not made by Apple.
glossary.GPU acceleration: Using a computer's graphics hardware to make graphics work faster.
glossary.ARM: A family of processor designs used in computers and other devices.
glossary.SBC: Single-board computer: a whole small computer built onto one board.
glossary.x86: A family of chip designs used in many personal computers.
glossary.deepfake: A fake video or audio made to look or sound like a real person.
glossary.Section 230: A US law that often protects websites from being legally responsible for what users post.
glossary.WebGL2: A browser feature that lets websites draw interactive 3D scenes.
glossary.contenteditable: A webpage setting that lets people edit text directly on the page.
glossary.DOM: Document Object Model: the browser's list of the pieces that make up a webpage.
glossary.codec: A set of rules that shrinks video for storage or sending and turns it back into a playable picture.
glossary.ULC: Ultra Low Complexity Codec: an audio format built to take little computing work to decode.
glossary.RSP: Reality Signal Processor: the N64 helper processor used for jobs including sound and graphics.
glossary.RSPL: A small C-like language used to write code for the N64's RSP.
glossary.IMDCT: Inverse Modified Discrete Cosine Transform: a math step that turns the decoder's numbers into sound samples.
glossary.RDP: Reality Display Processor: the N64 graphics hardware that draws the picture.
glossary.fillrate: How quickly graphics hardware can draw and fill parts of a picture.
glossary.correction territory: A market is in correction territory when it has fallen 10% or more from a recent high.
glossary.data-center buildout: The work of building more large facilities that house computers used to store data and run online services.
glossary.Nasdaq Composite: A stock-market index that tracks many companies listed on the Nasdaq exchange.
glossary.VAE: Variational Autoencoder: an AI that learns to squeeze information into a simpler form, then use it to create new examples.
glossary.latent space: A model's internal workspace for handling information without writing it out as words.
glossary.latent diffusion: A picture-making approach where the model works on a compressed version of image data instead of directly on pixels.
glossary.convergence: When training settles into a useful pattern and the model’s results stop changing as much.
glossary.model weights: The learned settings inside an AI that shape how it responds.
glossary.attention context window: The amount of information a model can consider at one time while generating an answer.
glossary.informant: A regular person recruited to pass information to the secret police; being listed does not prove they actually filed reports.
glossary.agent: An AI system that can take steps and use tools to get a task done, not just answer questions.
glossary.cochlear implant: A device that sends electrical signals to help someone hear.
glossary.psychophysics: A way of studying how physical things, like sound, relate to what a person senses.
glossary.Lean 4: A programming language and tool for checking that mathematical reasoning follows rules.
glossary.Mixture-of-Experts: A model made of specialist parts that only uses some of them for each request.
glossary.active parameters: The portion of an AI model it uses to produce each piece of an answer.
glossary.open weights: The model's learned settings are available for people to download and run themselves.
glossary.Apache 2.0: A set of legal terms that lets people use and share software, subject to its conditions.
glossary.AI trade: Investing in companies because you expect AI to make them more valuable.
glossary.buy the dip: Buying a stock after its price falls, hoping it will rise later.
